classification.difficultyReason: Recall the theorem and viewing-angle definitions, then represent elevation and depression on one line-of-sight diagram with horizontal references.

questions.mappingNote: Source parts (a)–(d) map individually to the four response children; F1 on teacher page 37 matches all four tasks.
questions.methodNote: Definition recall and a labelled line-of-sight construction; no teaching pages were supplied.

classification.difficultyReason: Recall the opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse ratios; the sine numerator is already supplied and no calculation or method selection is needed.

questions.mappingNote: The three source columns map to parts (a), (b), (c); the supplied sine numerator remains visible. Teacher F2 confirms all three ratios.
questions.methodNote: Recall the opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse definitions of the three right-triangle ratios.

classification.difficultyReason: Recall each reciprocal identity and identify its nonzero denominator condition using the supplied fraction and condition scaffolds.

questions.mappingNote: Each source row retains its denominator blank and separate condition blank. F3(b) in the key prints only the condition; the missing denominator is supplied mathematically.
questions.methodNote: Use reciprocal identities and exclude zero denominators.

classification.difficultyReason: Recall the starting directions and acute-angle convention for compass bearings, and clockwise measurement from north with three-digit notation for true bearings.

questions.mappingNote: Source parts (a) and (b) match teacher F4(a) and F4(b). The ambiguous word 'respectively' in the compass-bearing key is omitted from the authored answer.
questions.methodNote: Describe compass bearings from north or south towards east or west, and true bearings clockwise from north using three digits.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify the hypotenuse in each supplied right triangle, choose addition or subtraction of squares, and take the positive square root.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts directly assess missing sides of right-angled triangles.
questions.methodNote: Teaching evidence unavailable. The right-angle marks support using Pythagoras' theorem, taking the positive square root for a length.

classification.difficultyReason: Complete each Pythagorean triad by recognising the triple or taking the square root of the sum of the two supplied squares.

questions.mappingNote: Each part assesses the missing largest member of a Pythagorean triad.
questions.methodNote: Teaching evidence unavailable. Complete each integer triad using Pythagoras' theorem.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate supplied ratios in degree mode; the hardest parts combine converting minutes to degrees with taking the appropriate reciprocal and rounding to two decimal places.

questions.mappingNote: Calculator trigonometry is the closest available catalogue fit. Parts a–c use direct ratios; d–f use reciprocal ratios.
questions.methodNote: Teaching evidence unavailable. Evaluate in degree mode, convert minutes using 60 minutes per degree, and express secant, cosecant and cotangent as reciprocals.

classification.difficultyReason: For the hardest parts, convert a reciprocal ratio to sine, cosine or tangent, apply the corresponding inverse function on the acute domain, and convert the result to degrees and minutes.

questions.mappingNote: Finding angles with inverse ratios is the closest available fit to trig-practical-problems; acute-angle restrictions are retained.
questions.methodNote: Teaching evidence unavailable. Use inverse trigonometric functions in degree mode; convert reciprocal ratios first and round the resulting angle to the nearest minute.

classification.difficultyReason: Select the appropriate side ratio in each triangle; the hardest part simplifies x/x² to 1/x before solving for a positive length.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a, b and c directly assess sine, tangent and cosine respectively; c also requires simplifying x/x squared.
questions.methodNote: Teaching evidence unavailable. Select the ratio from the opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse labels, substitute, rearrange and round only the final value.

classification.difficultyReason: Keep the pole length fixed, calculate the original and new horizontal distances using Pythagoras, then subtract them to find the movement.

questions.mappingNote: Part a establishes the original distance used by part b; both remain within the same question and share all givens.
questions.methodNote: Teaching evidence unavailable. Apply Pythagoras' theorem to the original and slipped positions, retaining the fixed pole length, then subtract the horizontal distances.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify the height as opposite and the ground distance as adjacent, then apply sine and cosine directly to the given hypotenuse.

questions.mappingNote: Both requested perpendicular lengths directly assess practical right-triangle trigonometry.
questions.methodNote: Teaching pages were not supplied. The solution uses sine for the opposite side and cosine for the adjacent side, with the given hypotenuse.

classification.difficultyReason: Find the missing hypotenuse with Pythagoras, then identify opposite and adjacent sides for two different angles and use ordinary and reciprocal ratio definitions.

questions.mappingNote: The most advanced assessed task is evaluating trigonometric and reciprocal ratios. The closest supplied catalogue skill is trig-practical-problems; Pythagoras is secondary.
questions.methodNote: No teaching pages supplied. Part (a) explicitly requires Pythagoras’ theorem; part (b) uses side-ratio definitions, including reciprocal ratios.

classification.difficultyReason: Represent each named angle using a horizontal reference and an ascending or descending line of sight, placing the supplied angle at the observer.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts assess the geometric representation of elevation or depression.
questions.methodNote: Teaching context unavailable. Each angle is measured at the observer from a horizontal reference towards the line of sight, as confirmed by the keyed diagrams.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the supplied right-triangle diagram to identify opposite and adjacent sides, select tangent, rearrange for the horizontal distance and round.

questions.mappingNote: The source explicitly gives an angle of elevation and a cliff height, directly matching elevation-depression.
questions.methodNote: No teaching pages supplied. Tangent relates the given opposite side to the required adjacent horizontal distance.

classification.difficultyReason: Find the shared pole height with tangent, then use that unrounded height in the second right triangle to determine the other ground distance.

questions.mappingNote: The two elevations and the pole-to-A distance directly assess elevation problems with a shared vertical height.
questions.methodNote: Teaching pages were not supplied. Solutions use the tangent ratio in the two right triangles and retain the unrounded shared height.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate the opposite-side observation points into two right triangles, calculate each horizontal distance using tangent and recognise that the distances must be added.

questions.mappingNote: The tower height and two angles of elevation determine the distance between opposite-side observation points.
questions.methodNote: Teaching pages were not supplied. Apply tangent separately to the two right triangles, then add the horizontal distances.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate depression and elevation into two right triangles, use tangent to find the horizontal distance, then reuse it and add the observer's 6 m elevation to obtain the total wall height.

questions.mappingNote: The lower sight line determines horizontal distance; the upper sight line determines the additional height above the observer.
questions.methodNote: Teaching pages were not supplied. Use equal elevation/depression angles and tangent; the total wall height includes the 6 m observation height.

classification.difficultyReason: Read each labelled angle from south, identify east or west, and subtract from or add to 180 degrees to express the clockwise bearing from north.

questions.mappingNote: Each supplied sector starts at south, directly assessing compass-to-true bearing conversion.
questions.methodNote: Student teaching pages were not supplied. Inspected supplemental answer page 37, F4: compass bearings start at north or south; true bearings are measured clockwise from north and written with three digits.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert the given angle from west to its complement from north, interpret the reverse direction using the parallel compass axes, and express both directions as compass and true bearings.

questions.mappingNote: Both original directions are printed on page 6. The shared diagram on page 5 supplies the 40-degree angle needed for both bearings.
questions.methodNote: Student teaching pages were not supplied. Inspected supplemental answer page 37, F4, for compass-bearing and true-bearing conventions. Use complementary angles and clockwise angles from north.

classification.difficultyReason: Represent the verbal town positions as a right triangle, convert the 300-degree bearing to the 60-degree interior angle at B, and select cosine to find the hypotenuse from the adjacent distance.

questions.mappingNote: The town positions establish a right angle at A; the given northward distance is adjacent to the angle at B.
questions.methodNote: Teaching pages were not supplied. Independently solved using the bearing to identify a 60-degree angle and applying cosine in a right-angled triangle.

classification.difficultyReason: Represent the perpendicular north and east displacements as a right triangle, select inverse tangent for the angle east of north, and express the rounded result as a true bearing.

questions.mappingNote: The northward and eastward displacements are perpendicular. The answer-book F4(b) definition on PDF page 37 supports three-digit true-bearing notation.
questions.methodNote: Teaching pages were not supplied. Independently solved using inverse tangent for the angle east of north.

classification.difficultyReason: Introduce a perpendicular to split the supplied route into two right triangles, convert the bearing and south-east direction into usable angles, then combine their horizontal lengths using the height found in part (a).

questions.mappingNote: Part (a) finds the common perpendicular height; part (b) finds and adds the two horizontal components, retaining exact values until rounding.
questions.methodNote: Teaching pages were not supplied. The source question explicitly requires two triangles; both solutions use the perpendicular from B to AC.

classification.difficultyReason: Infer a right angle from the difference between the two bearings, identify the required distance as the hypotenuse, and apply Pythagoras.

questions.mappingNote: The bearings determine perpendicular rays OP and OQ, so PQ is the hypotenuse. The answer-book F1(a) on PDF page 37 confirms the Pythagorean relationship.
questions.methodNote: Teaching pages were not supplied. Independently solved by subtracting the bearings and applying Pythagoras' theorem.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert compass and reverse bearings to establish the right angle, then use the scaffolded distance and angle calculations to reconstruct the clockwise bearing of the final displacement and its reciprocal.

questions.mappingNote: The shared ship journey supplies all four parts. Part (d) directly assesses true bearings, with distance and inverse trigonometry supporting the result.
questions.methodNote: Teaching pages were not supplied. Independently solved using reverse bearings, Pythagoras' theorem, tangent and the angle sum of a triangle; conformity with the textbook's worked method remains unverified.

classification.difficultyReason: Use equal horizontal distances to express two tangent ratios, rearrange for BC, substitute into the supplied preceding result, and subtract the height difference from h. The three show-that parts explicitly guide the symbolic argument.

questions.mappingNote: The shared tower diagram supplies all three parts. The most advanced directly assessed relationship is symbolic application of tangent to angles of depression.
questions.methodNote: Teaching pages were not supplied. The question itself prescribes tangent ratios, finding BC first in part (b), and subtracting DE from CE in part (c). Independently authored proofs follow that sequence.

classification.difficultyReason: Complete two special triangles using Pythagoras, then reinterpret their sides relative to each acute angle to derive the ratio table; the supplied diagrams and 'Hence' scaffold this routine linked procedure.

questions.mappingNote: The two triangles and the word 'Hence' establish the local derivation. No separate teaching pages were supplied.
questions.methodNote: Pythagoras completes the two special triangles; opposite/hypotenuse, adjacent/hypotenuse and opposite/adjacent then give the table.

classification.difficultyReason: Select the known special-angle and secant values, substitute them into explicit expressions, and simplify squares, products and sums of fractions and surds; no unsignposted identity or representation change is required.

questions.mappingNote: Fundamentals 1 on the assigned page establishes the special-angle values. Question 1 establishes the reciprocal-ratio application. Separate teaching pages were not supplied.
questions.methodNote: Substitute exact special-angle ratios and simplify using exact fraction and surd arithmetic. Reciprocal ratios supply secant values.

classification.difficultyReason: Represent the supplied sine ratio with a right triangle, then follow explicit prompts to apply Pythagoras and read off cosine and tangent.

questions.mappingNote: The supplied sine ratio determines opposite side 2 and hypotenuse 3; part (b) determines the adjacent side used by both leaves of part (c).
questions.methodNote: The question explicitly teaches a right-triangle construction, Pythagoras’ Theorem and then right-triangle ratios. Separate teaching pages were not supplied.

classification.difficultyReason: Transfer the preceding triangle method to each supplied ratio, identify the appropriate sides including cotangent and cosecant, find the missing side with Pythagoras and form the requested ratio.

questions.mappingNote: Each part supplies its own ratio and acute-angle condition through the shared stem. The reference to Question 4 concerns method, so Question 5 remains a separate selectable question.
questions.methodNote: Use the triangle-and-Pythagoras technique explicitly scaffolded in Question 4 on the inspected source page. Separate teaching pages were not supplied.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify the required segment in nested right triangles, combine the supplied angles, calculate two lengths using exact ratios and subtract them; the equilateral part also requires constructing an altitude.

questions.mappingNote: Part (a) assesses a single exact-ratio calculation; (b) assesses equilateral height; (c) and (d) assess differences of lengths in nested right triangles. Unknown x is attached to the source-specific segment or height in every figure.
questions.methodNote: Use exact special-angle ratios and right-triangle geometry. Part (b) uses the perpendicular bisector of the base of an equilateral triangle and Pythagoras’ Theorem. Separate teaching pages were not supplied.

classification.difficultyReason: Follow the supplied double-angle identity to form and solve a quadratic, select its positive root using the acute angle, then transfer the scaffolded method to 22.5 degrees.

questions.mappingNote: The embedded identity and parts (a)–(c) directly scaffold the method reused in part (d). No separate teaching pages were supplied.
questions.methodNote: Use the tangent double-angle identity supplied inside the question, rearrange to a quadratic and select the positive root because the angle is acute.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute into the supplied double-angle identity, rearrange for sine and select the positive root, then connect the prompted surd expansion to the nested radical. The explicit intermediate targets scaffold this linked algebraic derivation.

questions.mappingNote: The embedded identity is retained in the parent prompt. The explicit progression from parts (a) and (b) to part (c) determines the solution method. No separate teaching pages were supplied.
questions.methodNote: Use the supplied cosine double-angle identity, select the positive sine value and use the requested surd expansion to simplify the nested radical.

classification.difficultyReason: Recall the positive and negative rotation directions, with initial-letter cues; no calculation or linked reasoning is required.

questions.mappingNote: Both source statements directly assess angle-measurement direction. Separate teaching pages were not supplied.
questions.methodNote: Use the conventional positive anti-clockwise and negative clockwise directions of rotation.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise supplementary angles and distinguish preserved ratio magnitude from quadrant-dependent sign, with initial-letter cues.

questions.mappingNote: Part a assesses supplementary-angle terminology; part b assesses the magnitude/sign distinction for 180°±θ and 360°±θ. Separate teaching pages were not supplied.
questions.methodNote: Use the sum of supplementary angles and the related-angle rule: retain the ratio magnitude and determine its sign from the quadrant.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify the axis point reached by a positive or negative quarter-turn multiple, then read its sine or cosine coordinate from the supplied unit circle.

questions.mappingNote: All sixteen parts evaluate sine or cosine at axis angles. The permanent diagram supplies the required coordinate definitions; no separate teaching pages were supplied.
questions.methodNote: Use the supplied unit-circle definitions: cosine is the x-coordinate and sine is the y-coordinate. Positive turns are anticlockwise and negative turns clockwise.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the supplied symmetric circle to determine which coordinates change sign under reflections or a half-turn, and combine those signs for tangent.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–c use reflection in the y-axis, d–f a half-turn, g–i reflection in the x-axis, and j–l negative-angle reflection. Separate teaching evidence was not supplied.
questions.methodNote: Use the supplied circle's reflection symmetry. Sine follows the y-coordinate, cosine follows the x-coordinate, and tangent is their quotient.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify opposite and adjacent sides for the two supplied complementary angles, then express the resulting ratios as cosine, sine and cotangent of x.

questions.mappingNote: All three parts directly assess complementary-angle relationships; the side ratios justify the key answers.
questions.methodNote: Teaching evidence unavailable. Use the supplied triangle to identify opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse for the complementary angles.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply a complementary-angle identity to each equation and subtract the given angle from 90 degrees; the acute-angle condition selects the unique required value.

questions.mappingNote: The four equations require complementary-angle relationships, with the acute condition selecting the intended angle.
questions.methodNote: Teaching evidence unavailable. Replace each ratio by its complementary-angle equivalent and use the acute-angle condition.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise reciprocal products and cancel them; the final part requires expressing cot x as cos x divided by sin x before cancellation.

questions.mappingNote: The nearest supplied catalogue skill is trig-ratio definitions; reciprocal identities are directly assessed but have no dedicated supplied skill.
questions.methodNote: Teaching evidence unavailable. Use reciprocal and quotient definitions to simplify each product.

classification.difficultyReason: Select complementary-angle substitutions, sometimes combine them with a reciprocal identity, then simplify products, differences or fractional expressions by combining like terms and cancelling common factors.

questions.mappingNote: Every pair of angles sums to 90 degrees; preserve the source's two-column, row-major order.
questions.methodNote: Teaching evidence unavailable. Use complementary-angle relationships, then combine like terms or cancel reciprocal factors.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify each related acute angle, determine the ratio's quadrant sign and apply a standard exact value; the parts require repeated direct applications without an additional connection or unfamiliar representation.

questions.mappingNote: Twelve expressions retain the source's four-column row order; quadrant-form evaluation is the most advanced directly assessed supplied skill.
questions.methodNote: Teaching evidence unavailable. Use the related acute angle, quadrant sign and standard exact values.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise one or two complete turns and retain the same sine or cosine coordinate; the unit-circle method is explicitly requested.

questions.mappingNote: Four expressions assess trig definitions for angles differing by complete revolutions.
questions.methodNote: Teaching evidence unavailable. Explain periodicity through complete turns and unchanged unit-circle coordinates, as the prompt requests.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert each supplied angle to exact unit-circle coordinates using reference angles and quadrant signs, including using the diagram to select the negative y-coordinate for S.

questions.mappingNote: The page-13 shared stem and diagram combine with all four page-14 conditions. The diagram resolves S as quadrant IV, so the printed 30-degree angle is a clockwise reference angle.
questions.methodNote: Teaching evidence unavailable. Use unit-circle coordinates (cos theta, sin theta), exact reference-angle values and quadrant signs.

classification.difficultyReason: Find an unknown coordinate from the unit-circle equation, select its sign from the quadrant, then connect coordinate ratios to related-angle expressions; the staged parts supply the intermediate results.

questions.mappingNote: The two source groups and eight Roman-numbered tasks are retained. The referenced circle's givens are repeated so this separately selectable printed question is self-contained.
questions.methodNote: Teaching evidence unavailable. Use x²+y²=1, select the root using the quadrant, and apply unit-circle ratio definitions and related-angle signs.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply negative-angle relationships and exact reference-angle values; the hardest part reduces −585 degrees to a coterminal angle before selecting the sine value.

questions.mappingNote: All six printed negative-angle expressions directly assess the supplied negative-angle skill; part f also uses complete turns.
questions.methodNote: Teaching evidence unavailable. Use negative-angle identities, coterminal angles and exact reference-angle values.

classification.difficultyReason: Reduce each angle by complete revolutions, identify the reference angle and quadrant sign, and recall the exact special-angle ratio.

questions.mappingNote: All six angles exceed one revolution; exact evaluation retains the source three-column row order.
questions.methodNote: Teaching evidence unavailable. Subtract complete revolutions, then use the related angle and quadrant sign.

classification.difficultyReason: Read angles measured from different axis directions, associate cosine and sine with the two coordinates, and apply the quadrant signs while retaining exact trigonometric forms.

questions.mappingNote: The three requested points form one unpartitioned source response; no new printed subparts are introduced.
questions.methodNote: Teaching evidence unavailable. Express unit-circle coordinates using reference-angle sine and cosine and the quadrant signs; retain exact trigonometric forms.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute the supplied angles into each side independently, evaluate exact ratios with quadrant signs, and simplify products and squares to demonstrate equal values.

questions.mappingNote: The identities are permanent question givens. This task verifies particular values rather than proving general identities; the closest supplied skill is exact quadrant-form evaluation.
questions.methodNote: Teaching evidence unavailable. Evaluate the left and right sides independently by substituting the given angles and exact trigonometric values, then compare.

classification.difficultyReason: Transform related and complementary angles to ratios of one angle, then select reciprocal, quotient or Pythagorean identities to simplify products, sums and fractions.

questions.mappingNote: Each of the six expressions directly assesses transformation to ratios of the same angle before simplification.
questions.methodNote: Teaching pages were not supplied. Authored working uses related-angle and complementary-angle relationships, reciprocal ratios and the Pythagorean identity.

classification.difficultyReason: Select complementary, supplementary and negative-angle identities for four factors, track the negative denominator, and recognise the resulting quotient as negative tangent squared; the target guides the routine proof.

questions.mappingNote: The supplied identity is verified directly; no general addition formula is needed.
questions.methodNote: Teaching pages were not supplied. Transform the left-hand side using complementary-angle, supplementary-angle and negative-angle identities, then use the quotient identity.

classification.difficultyReason: Check related-angle identities, then combine quadrant and reciprocal relationships to show that the final two expressions reduce to 1 and a positive reciprocal square before judging the inequalities.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–d test identities; parts e–f test the sign after simplification. Identities and inequalities are assessed where the expressions are defined.
questions.methodNote: Teaching pages were not supplied. Check each statement using related-angle, complementary-angle, negative-angle and reciprocal relationships.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the given ratio and sign conditions to select the correct square-root sign, recover a missing ratio with the Pythagorean identity, and form a quotient; part (c) also requires first converting cosecant to sine.

questions.mappingNote: Each part supplies one ratio and sign or quadrant information and independently requests other exact ratios.
